params.question: What is the role of KNDy neurons (kisspeptin, neurokinin B, dynorphin) in the initiation of puberty?

answers.text: They suppress GnRH pulsatility during childhood; puberty begins when this suppression lifts

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. KNDy neurons in the arcuate nucleus act as the GnRH pulse generator. During childhood their activity is suppressed, keeping GnRH, LH, and FSH low. At puberty, this suppression lifts, allowing pulsatile GnRH release that activates the reproductive axis.

answers.text: They directly stimulate ovarian follicular development at the onset of puberty

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. KNDy neurons act at the hypothalamic level to regulate GnRH pulsatility — they do not directly stimulate the ovary. Ovarian stimulation occurs downstream via pituitary gonadotrophins (LH and FSH).

answers.text: They produce oestradiol that triggers the pubertal growth spurt

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. KNDy neurons are hypothalamic neurons that regulate GnRH secretion — they do not produce oestradiol. Oestradiol is produced by the ovary in response to gonadotrophins.

answers.text: They inhibit anterior pituitary FSH release until menarche occurs

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. KNDy neurons modulate GnRH release from the hypothalamus, not FSH from the pituitary. When their suppression lifts at puberty, pulsatile GnRH drives both LH and FSH release — well before menarche.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the HPO axis cascade: KNDy neurons in the arcuate nucleus regulate GnRH pulsatility. During childhood they are suppressed; at puberty the suppression lifts, starting the hormonal cascade.
Well done! KNDy neurons are the master switch — their reactivation at puberty initiates the entire HPO axis cascade.

params.question: A child presents with breast development at age 6 years but has suppressed (pre-pubertal) LH and FSH levels. Which of the following best explains this combination of findings?

answers.text: The hypothalamus has activated GnRH pulsatility prematurely, driving gonadotrophin release

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. If the hypothalamus had activated GnRH prematurely (central precocious puberty), LH and FSH would be elevated, not suppressed. Suppressed gonadotrophins point to a peripheral source of oestrogen.

answers.text: Autonomous peripheral oestrogen production is driving breast development independently of the HPO axis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Breast development with suppressed LH and FSH indicates peripheral precocious puberty — oestrogen is being produced autonomously (e.g., from an ovarian cyst, tumour, or exogenous exposure) without HPO axis activation.

answers.text: This is a normal variant of premature thelarche requiring no investigation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While premature thelarche is a benign variant, breast development at age 6 warrants investigation. The suppressed gonadotrophins specifically suggest a peripheral oestrogen source that must be identified.

answers.text: The anterior pituitary is directly secreting oestradiol without gonadotrophin mediation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The anterior pituitary secretes gonadotrophins (LH and FSH), not oestradiol. Oestradiol is produced by the ovary or other peripheral sources. The framework requires correctly identifying the anatomical level of dysfunction.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the framework: puberty is a cascade with multiple levels. The combination of secondary sexual characteristics PLUS suppressed central hormones (LH, FSH) points to autonomous peripheral hormone production, not central activation.

Excellent analysis! Matching the clinical picture (breast development) with the biochemical profile (suppressed gonadotrophins) localises the dysfunction to a peripheral source — exactly how the framework guides investigation.

params.question: A 14-year-old girl presents with no breast development (Tanner B1). Investigations reveal a bone age of 11 years, low serum LH and FSH that rise appropriately on GnRH stimulation, and a normal karyotype. What is the most appropriate initial management?

answers.text: Immediate initiation of combined oestrogen-progesterone hormone replacement therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. These findings (delayed bone age, low but responsive gonadotrophins, normal karyotype) are consistent with constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP), in which spontaneous puberty will occur. HRT is reserved for permanent gonadal failure such as Turner syndrome.

answers.text: Reassurance and watchful waiting, as the findings are consistent with constitutional delay

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The bone age delay, appropriately low gonadotrophins that respond to GnRH stimulation, and normal karyotype all point to CDGP. Spontaneous puberty will occur — the only issue is timing. Reassurance and periodic follow-up are first-line.

answers.text: Urgent referral for MRI brain to exclude a pituitary tumour

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The pituitary responds normally to GnRH stimulation, indicating intact gonadotroph function. MRI would be indicated if gonadotrophins were undetectable and failed to respond to GnRH, suggesting a structural hypothalamic-pituitary lesion.

answers.text: Surgical exploration of the pelvis to assess for gonadal dysgenesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The normal karyotype and responsive gonadotrophins argue against gonadal dysgenesis. Surgical exploration would only be considered if imaging suggested absent or streak gonads in the setting of a 46,XY karyotype.

overallFeedback.feedback: The combination of delayed bone age + low-but-responsive gonadotrophins + normal karyotype = constitutional delay of growth and puberty (CDGP). Management is reassurance, not intervention — spontaneous puberty will follow.
Well done! Recognising CDGP and distinguishing it from pathological causes of delayed puberty is a key clinical skill — it avoids unnecessary investigation and inappropriate hormone therapy.

interactions.label: A 7-year-old girl presents with Tanner B3 breast development, pubic hair, and ac

params.question: A 7-year-old girl presents with Tanner B3 breast development, pubic hair, and accelerated growth velocity. LH and FSH are elevated and rise further on GnRH stimulation testing. MRI brain is normal. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

answers.text: Surgical exploration to identify and remove an ovarian hormone-secreting tumour

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The elevated and GnRH-responsive gonadotrophins indicate central precocious puberty (premature HPO axis activation), not peripheral autonomous hormone production. Surgery targets peripheral causes such as ovarian tumours, where gonadotrophins would be suppressed.

answers.text: Low-dose combined oral contraceptive pill to regulate the early menstrual cycle

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. OCPs do not address the underlying premature HPO axis activation and would not preserve height potential. The goal in central precocious puberty is to suppress the axis and allow the child to reach her genetically programmed adult height.

answers.text: GnRH analogue therapy (e.g., leuprolide) to suppress premature HPO axis activation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. GnRH analogues are first-line for central precocious puberty. They work by providing continuous (non-pulsatile) GnRH stimulation, which downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors and abolishes LH/FSH release — halting pubertal progression and preserving adult height.

answers.text: An aromatase inhibitor (e.g., letrozole) to block peripheral oestrogen synthesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Aromatase inhibitors block peripheral oestrogen conversion but do not suppress the central HPO axis. They may have a role in peripheral precocious puberty (e.g., McCune-Albright syndrome), not in centrally driven cases with elevated gonadotrophins.

overallFeedback.feedback: In central precocious puberty (elevated LH/FSH that respond to GnRH), first-line treatment is GnRH analogues. They convert pulsatile stimulation to continuous, downregulating pituitary receptors and halting the premature cascade.

Excellent! GnRH analogues exploit a pharmacological paradox: continuous GnRH stimulation downregulates the very receptors that pulsatile GnRH activates, effectively switching off the prematurely triggered HPO axis.
